clusters.title: Body read (and fetch await) not raced against the bounded signal: a stalled body that ignores abort hangs past requestTimeoutMs
clusters.claim: requestTimeoutMs and the owner abort exist only as the AbortSignal.any signal built in bounded() (src/main/github-oauth.ts:97-99) and passed to the fetcher as init.signal. readBounded's `await reader.read()` (l.108-115, reached from classify l.162 and loginOf l.212) never observes that signal. Some members also cite `await sent` in classify (l.154) and loginOf (l.210), so a fetcher promise that never settles is not raced either. An injected fetcher that ignores init.signal and returns a body that stalls (or never resolves) leaves requestToken, requestDeviceCode and fetchLogin pending forever. Members say this breaks spec 5.1 (every request bounded by requestTimeoutMs) and 5.3 row 1 (timeout gives transient, failed at step 1, or null for the login). They note the shipped stalled-body tests use real fetch over the loopback fake, which honours the signal. One member adds that zero-length chunks are read without limit, and one says the spec does not state whether honouring init.signal is part of the Fetcher contract.

clusters.title: Awaited body/reader cancel() has no bound: a cancel that never settles holds back an already-decided result
clusters.claim: Every body cancel is awaited with no time bound: the declared-oversize path at src/main/github-oauth.ts:110 (response.body?.cancel()), readBounded's finally at l.119 (reader.cancel(); one member cites l.122), classify's finally at l.171 for 3xx and rate-limited answers, and loginOf's non-2xx path at l.211. ReadableStream.cancel() settles only when the source's cancel does. So an injected Response body whose cancel never settles keeps the call pending, even when the result is already known (429 rate-limited, unusable 302, declared or streamed oversize, 401 to fetchLogin). Neither requestTimeoutMs nor an owner abort can end it. Members say spec 5.1 requires the body to be cancelled or released, not awaited, and that the 'body always cancelled' rule becomes a liveness hole. This is reachable only through an injected Fetcher's custom stream.

clusters.title: Combined: the body phase (read and cancel) never observes the timeout signal, so a stalled stream or a never-settling cancel hangs the call
clusters.claim: These findings make both claims in one: readBounded/classify/loginOf neither race `await reader.read()` (src/main/github-oauth.ts:115) against the bounded() signal (l.97-99), nor bound the awaited cancels (reader.cancel() at l.119; response.body?.cancel() at l.110, l.171, l.211). The timeout and owner abort reach the body only if the fetcher wires init.signal into the stream. So an injected Response body that stalls, or whose cancel() never settles (for example on an oversize body or a 429), never settles the call after requestTimeoutMs fires. Members say this breaks 5.1 and 5.3 row 1 (timeout gives transient), and that the shipped tests only cover stalls through real fetch/undici. One member calls this a spec gap: 5.1 and 5.3 do not say whether the wire or the fetcher enforces the timeout during the body read.

clusters.title: ERROR_CODE /^[a-z_]{1,64}$/ lets a token-shaped error value through verbatim as the result code
clusters.claim: classify row 5 (src/main/github-oauth.ts:165-166) returns the response's `error` value as the result's code whenever it matches ERROR_CODE = /^[a-z_]{1,64}$/ (cited at l.32 and at l.16). That regex admits a lowercase, all-letter token-shaped string such as 'ghu_abcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyz', so a token or response text can reach a result. Members say this breaks spec 3.9 layer 1 and DC-9 (no result carries GitHub's response text or a token). Members say it is hypothetical: GitHub would have to echo a token into `error`, and real tokens usually contain digits, which the regex refuses. One member notes the regex is quoted from spec 3.5 and 5.3 row 5, so this is a spec gap as well.

clusters.title: parseBody's flat-object check rejects a 2xx token answer that has a boolean or null field
clusters.claim: parseBody (src/main/github-oauth.ts:136) type-checks every value of the JSON body and rejects the whole 2xx answer when any field is a boolean or null. A valid token answer carrying an extra field such as "flag": true therefore becomes transient, and the access token is lost. The member says this contradicts spec 5.3, under which error_description, error_uri and every other field are dropped unread, as against row 4's flat-object rule.

lenses.scratchTest: tests/zz-adj-C-1-reproduce.test.ts (uncommitted; 3/3 pass in 3.5 s). With requestTimeoutMs 50 and an injected Fetcher that ignores init.signal and returns `new Response(stalledStream, {status:200, content-type: application/json})`, the test first checks `seen[0].signal.aborted === true` (the bounded signal fired). It then checks `expect(await within(tokenP, 1000)).toBe(PENDING)`, and does the same for requestDeviceCode and fetchLogin. A second test shows the same PENDING result when the fetcher's promise never settles. Every call is settled afterwards: closing the stream gives transient / failed / null. A control fetcher that errors its body stream on abort gets { kind: 'transient' } within the timeout.
lenses.why: The timeout exists only as the AbortSignal built by bounded() (src/main/github-oauth.ts:97-99), which is passed to the fetcher as init.signal (l.65 and l.91). Nothing in the module observes it. Neither `await sent` (classify l.154, loginOf l.210) nor readBounded's `await reader.read()` (l.112) is raced against it. The test confirmed that the signal was aborted at 50 ms while all three public functions were still pending at 1000 ms. Spec 5.1 bounds every request by requestTimeoutMs, and 5.3 row 1 says "the timeout fired → transient" (step 1: failed; the login: null). Under this input, neither result arrives. The only input needed was a Response from an injected Fetcher (Fetcher type, src/main/github-credential.ts:5), and the spec does not require a Fetcher to honour init.signal. The module was not edited. I rate it S3, not higher: the shipped lateFetch (real fetch) aborts both the fetch and its body stream on the signal, so production calls are bounded. The hang needs a non-conforming fetcher or a body stream that ignores abort.

Admissible input: Fetcher is `(url, init) => Promise<Response>` (src/main/inference.ts:14, spec 3.4 l.262), and its contract does not say it must honour init.signal. So a fetcher that ignores init.signal is admissible. It can return `new Response(new ReadableStream({ pull: () => new Promise(() => {}) }), { status: 200, headers: { 'content-type': 'application/json' } })`, or a promise that never settles. What forbids it: spec 5.3 row 1 says "the timeout fired" gives transient (failed at step 1, null for the login). Spec 5.1 bounds every request by requestTimeoutMs, and the module header (l.5) promises every failure comes back as a result kind. A promise that never settles breaks all three.
Why the tests miss it and how far it reaches: the shipped stalled-body tests (tests/github-oauth.test.ts:192-197, 240-246) use real fetch against the loopback fake, and real fetch errors the body stream when the signal aborts. Production passes lateFetch, which is globalThis.fetch (spec l.264), so the shipped app is not exposed; that is why I rate it S3, not higher. Under the run's definition it is still reachable with an injected fetcher. If it happens, the 6.5 refresh, which waits only on its own timeout (spec l.760-761), would never finish.

lenses.scratchTest: tests/zz-adj-C-2-reproduce.test.ts (uncommitted). For each of the five paths: `expect(await within(result, 400)).toBe(PENDING)` with requestTimeoutMs 50 and an owner abort at 60 ms, then `body.release()` followed by `expect(await within(result, 400)).toEqual(decided)`. 6/6 pass, control included.

All five cited paths stayed pending for 400 ms. That is 8x requestTimeoutMs, and the owner's AbortController had already fired. The five paths, each with the result it was holding: 429 gives rate-limited (classify finally, src/main/github-oauth.ts:171); 302 gives unusable/302 (l.171); a declared content-length of 999999 gives failed (readBounded l.110); a 2048-byte streamed chunk against maxBodyBytes 1024 gives transient (readBounded finally l.119); a 401 to fetchLogin gives null (loginOf l.211).
Each source's cancel() ran exactly once. Every call resolved to the already-decided value as soon as the test released cancel(), so the result was known and held back only by the awaited cancel.
The timeout and the abort cannot help: `bounded()` (l.97-98) only feeds the fetcher's init.signal, and once a Response exists, nothing in the module watches that signal.
This breaks spec 5.1 (docs/specification/github-sign-in.md:540-541: the signal bounds the request, and the body is 'cancelled or released', not awaited). It also breaks L-3 (l.123: a refresh ends 'only by its response or by its own 20 s timeout') and the table rows at l.162-165.

That regex admits a lowercase, all-letter token-shaped string such as 'ghu_abcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyz', so a token or response text can reach a result. Members say this breaks spec 3.9 layer 1 and DC-9 (no result carries GitHub's response text or a token). lenses.scratchTest: tests/zz-adj-C-4-reproduce.test.ts (passes, 1/1): expect(await requestToken(answering(400, { error: 'ghu_abcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyz' }), ...)).toEqual({ kind: 'error', code: 'ghu_abcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyz', intervalS: null }). The same result comes back for a 200 carrying `error` and for requestDeviceCode. As controls, a token containing digits and a 65-character value both map to 'unknown'.
lenses.why:
I observed the behaviour. classify row 5 (src/main/github-oauth.ts:165) returns the `error` string verbatim when it matches ERROR_CODE (l.32, /^[a-z_]{1,64}$/). tokenResult (l.~199) and deviceCodeResult (l.~185) then copy that string into the result's code. Reaching it took only a JSON Response from an injected Fetcher, which the contract admits, so it is reachable through requestToken and requestDeviceCode.
The specification itself prescribes this behaviour, though. Spec 5.3 row 5 (docs/specification/github-sign-in.md:579) and the 3.5 type comment (l.295, repeated at src/main/github-oauth.ts:18) say to pass `error` through when it matches ^[a-z_]{1,64}$ and to use 'unknown' otherwise. The `error` code is GitHub response text by nature, so this is a deliberate carve-out from 3.9 layer 1 (l.398, "never carry response text"). Layer 1 also "crosses nothing" (it stays inside main).
The leak is narrow. A real token contains digits and the regex refuses digits, as my control shows. A token-shaped value can only get through if GitHub echoes an all-letter, token-like string in `error`.
So the code matches its spec and the defect is at most a gap between spec 3.9 and 5.3. That is why I grade it S4 and do not count it as a code bug.

cluster.title: parseBody's flat-object check rejects a 2xx token answer that has a boolean or null field
cluster.claim: parseBody (src/main/github-oauth.ts:136) type-checks every value of the JSON body and rejects the whole 2xx answer when any field is a boolean or null. A valid token answer carrying an extra field such as "flag": true therefore becomes transient, and the access token is lost. The member says this contradicts spec 5.3, under which error_description, error_uri and every other field are dropped unread, as against row 4's flat-object rule.

Line 584 ("error_description, error_uri and every other field are dropped unread") is about fields of a body that has already passed row 4. Rows 5 and 6 never read them. It does not exempt any body from row 4's flat-object rule.
